old_title: Macron vows 'concrete' measures to address student demands after unrest
new_title: French students vow to continue protests despite concessions from Macron govt
old_text:
Macron vows 'concrete' measures to address student demands after unrest
French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday said the government will announce "concrete and strong" measures to address the demands by high school students after their protests demanding better education conditions triggered weeks of nationwide unrest. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is set to hold a news conference after meeting with high school student unions.
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday that his Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will announce "strong measures" to assuage French student protesters, while noting that next weekend could nevertheless bring the risk of more unrest.
"I have also asked the government to respond to the legitimate demands that lie at the root of this social movement," he told reporters in Marseille on Monday.
Lecornu is set to hold a news conference later Monday after meeting with unions of high school students.
During a visit to Marseille, Macron repeated what Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said earlier on Monday, namely that more protests are expected next Saturday.
The French government is seeking to draw a line under weeks of protests that have been marred by violence due to widespread anger over the rising cost of living, with nationwide demonstrations on October 17 degenerating into some of the country's worst rioting in years.
The demonstrations come at a critical moment for France, six months ahead of a presidential election to replace centrist Macron.
The frontrunner - far-right leader Marine le Pen - held an election rally in Orleans Sunday, a day after yet more demonstrations also saw some violent clashes on the sidelines.
She vowed to "restore the rule of law" if elected next year. Polls show the protests and ensuing disorder have boosted her support, as the government and Macron faced sharp criticism over the unrest.
Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes, large-scale looting and vandalism of public property that erupted on October 17, and had stepped up security for Saturday's protests.
While Nunez said the outcome of Saturday's rallies was more "positive" than a week ago, street violence still erupted in the French capital and a number of other cities including Marseille.

During his visit to Marseille, France's second-largest city, Macron made a stop at the city hall after it was damaged in the protest violence on October 17.
He also meets with shopkeepers who had fallen victim to looting and vandalism, according to the French presidential palace.
After this weekend's protests, many shopfronts in the city centre were still boarded up early Monday, just hours before Macron's arrival.
Macron's visit was intended to demonstrate that "the state is present, standing firm and fulfilling its mission to protect", an aide said.
'High level of violence'
A total of 1,435 people were arrested on the sidelines of the most recent weekend protests, Nunez said on Monday.
"The day was brought under control and there were no serious incidents," he told broadcaster BFMTV.
"Nevertheless, we saw a very high level of violence directed at the internal security forces," Nunez added.
He said that 267 police officers and gendarmes were injured, along with 150 protesters, including three who were seriously hurt in Toulouse, Reims and Clermont-Ferrand.
The unrest followed weeks of demonstrations by students campaigning for better learning conditions.
Several teenage protesters have been seriously injured and thousands arrested.
The police response to their demonstrations, which included blockades of schools, has been criticised as heavy-handed and sparked a broader movement against the cost of living and police violence.
In Paris on Monday, Lecornu meets student leaders, with National Education Minister Édouard Geffray and Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste joining him for the talks. Following that meeting, Geffray and Baptiste will hold a news conference.
Macron already met representatives of secondary school pupils last Friday, but they emerged from the talks urging students to keep protesting until the government put forward concrete proposals to address their demands.
On top of the protests, the country was last week shaken by a shooting that killed one person and wounded five, including a 12-year-old girl, outside Paris.
Macron has branded the shooting a "racist terrorist attack", as most of the victims were from foreign backgrounds.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)
new_text:
French students vow to continue protests despite concessions from Macron govt
French student leaders on Monday called for more protests despite President Emmanuel Macron's pledge of "concrete and strong" measures to address their demands after weeks of nationwide unrest. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu met with high school representatives alongside education ministers to announce follow-up action ranging from a total overhaul of higher education admissions platform Parcoursup to a cap on class sizes.
French student leaders vowed to go on protesting Monday despite government concessions on education, keeping pressure on President Emmanuel Macron as the movement spreads to unions and other activists, stokes unrest and deepens the economic damage.
The new measures included a commitment to cap the size of some high school classes; €4 billion ($4.5 billion) of loans for renovating schools; and the replacement by 2028 of a university admissions system students see as socially unfair.
"Not all our demands were met. We'll go on for as long as it takes," Louis Letoublon, one of the representatives of high school students, said as he and fellow student leaders emerged from a meeting with government officials in Paris.
The protests, which have broadened beyond education to draw in trade unions and yellow-vest activists, known for their high-visibility jackets, pose a test for Macron's minority government.
The government has little room to spend its way out of the unrest, with national debt approaching 120 percent of GDP, while the turmoil is boosting support for far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen ahead of next year's presidential election.
The package included €1 billion of investment in university campuses; a move to increase student grants with inflation; and the opening up of a further 15,000 higher education places for students.
"It's clear we have to ease the pressure being felt in the education system," Education Minister Edouard Geffray told a press conference.
There was no overall figure for how much funding the package would require. High borrowing needs are already complicating efforts to agree a budget for next year.
The protests, initially triggered by student discontent, have shown little sign of ending after violence nine days ago engulfed dozens of cities, leading to fears the state had lost control of the streets.
Earlier, Macron acknowledged it was likely there would be more unrest this weekend ahead of a bigger nationwide day of protests set for November 5.
On a tour to survey the damage in Marseille and to thank emergency services after Saturday's protests, he said he would keep security measures in place and work to move protests outside city centres.
Le Pen, already the frontrunner in next year's presidential election, has benefitted from the unrest and perceptions that authorities are struggling to keep the peace.
An opinion poll published on Sunday put her on 32 to 33.5 percent, well ahead of her nearest rival, hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon on 17 percent. Surveys suggest she would easily defeat Mélenchon in a run-off ballot, expected to be held in early May.
Far-right gangs confront far-left activists
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez earlier said that 1,435 people were arrested nationwide during demonstrations on Saturday and that police had also recorded a new phenomenon, with organised far-right gangs confronting far-left activists in several cities.
"We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements to come out, officially, to defend businesses," he said. "In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organised formations, mainly to target the ultra-left movement."
A selloff in French government bonds paused on Monday after rating agency Moody's on Friday refrained from downgrading the country's sovereign debt.
But business leaders said the unrest was continuing to inflict heavy economic damage.
Alain Di Crescenzo, head of the CCI France network of chambers of commerce and industry, said many retailers had remained closed as a precaution after the violence of October 17, adding this had led to sharp falls in sales.
"We have shopkeepers who are tired and demoralised, and we are killing local commerce," he told Radio Classique.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)
